target: Lo que me molesta es que nadie avisó.
english: What bothers me is that nobody gave notice.
tip: "Lo que" = what / the thing that: "Lo que dices es verdad" = What you say is true. For abstract or unspecified things.

target: Tengo la sensación de que algo va a pasar.
english: I have a feeling something is going to happen.
tip: 'The feeling that...' needs de: 'la sensación DE que algo va a pasar'. Noun + clause always takes de que – dropping that de is a classic native-level error too.

target: Cuantas más personas participen, más enriquecedor será el debate.
english: The more people participate, the more enriching the debate will be.
tip: 'The more..., the more...' loses both 'the's: 'Cuantas más personas participen, más...'. Cuanto agrees with the noun (cuantas ↔ personas), no article anywhere.

target: La razón por la que llegué tarde fue el tráfico.
english: The reason I arrived late was the traffic.
tip: English happily says 'the reason I arrived late,' dropping the link. Spanish can't: la razón POR la que – you must say the reason FOR which, or it sounds broken.

target: Hasta que no encuentre algo mejor, seguiré en este puesto.
english: Until I find something better, I will stay in this position.
tip: That no is not negative! 'Hasta que no encuentre algo mejor' still means 'until I FIND something better'. After hasta que, Spanish often adds a decorative no – ignore it.

target: El cliente con quien tengo la reunión llega a las tres.
english: The client I have the meeting with arrives at three.
tip: "Con quien" = with whom: "La persona con quien trabajo." Use preposition + quien when referring to people.

target: Si hubiera sabido que el hotel estaba tan lejos, habría alquilado un carro.
english: If I had known the hotel was so far, I would have rented a car.
tip: This is Spanish's regret formula: si hubiera sabido paints the past that never was, and habría alquilado names the outcome you missed. Both halves are needed.

target: De haber sabido las consecuencias, no habría aceptado.
english: Had I known the consequences, I would not have accepted.
tip: De haber + participle = formal alternative to si hubiera + participle.

target: Tanto si llueve como si hace sol, iremos de excursión.
english: Whether it rains or shines, we'll go on the excursion.
tip: 'Whether...or' = 'tanto si... como si': tanto si llueve como si hace sol – literally 'as much if it rains as if it's sunny'. The plan survives both options.

target: El autor, cuya obra fue premiada, dará una conferencia mañana.
english: The author, whose work was awarded, will give a lecture tomorrow.
tip: Cuyo agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'cuya obra' is feminine to match obra, even though el autor is masculine. Whose-words match forward in Spanish.

target: ¿De quién es este abrigo?
english: Whose coat is this?
tip: Spanish has no question-word for whose – cuyo never asks. You ask of whom: ¿De quién es este abrigo? = literally, of whom is this coat?

target: ¿Se lo has dicho ya?
english: Have you told him yet?
tip: Why se lo, not le lo? Spanish bans two l-pronouns back to back, so le shape-shifts into se before lo: ¿Se lo has dicho? = have you told him it?

target: El hotel fue renovado completamente.
english: The hotel was completely renovated.
tip: Fue renovado is the textbook passive – grammatical but formal. It lives in news and hotel brochures; in speech Spaniards would say se renovó. Match the register.

target: He comido demasiado, no puedo más.
english: I've eaten too much, I can't take any more.
tip: He comido is the Spain default for anything recent – today counts as 'now.' Much of Latin America would just say comí demasiado. Both fine; the dialects just differ on when the perfect is used.

target: Se come a las dos en España.
english: People eat lunch at two in Spain.
tip: A las dos for lunch is no typo: Spain really eats at 2pm and dines past 9. Restaurants at noon serve mostly tourists.

target: Agua que no has de beber, déjala correr.
english: If you can't drink it, let it flow.
tip: Agua que no has de beber, déjala correr – water you won't drink, let it run: mind your own business. Has de is an old-flavored must, alive mainly in sayings.

target: Digan lo que digan, voy a seguir adelante.
english: Whatever they say, I'm going to keep going.
tip: Digan lo que digan doubles the verb on purpose: subjunctive twice = no matter what they say. The repetition IS the grammar – say-what-they-may.

target: Se tarda una hora en llegar al aeropuerto.
english: It takes one hour to get to the airport.
tip: It takes an hour? Don't grab tomar – Spanish has a verb just for duration: tardar. Se tarda una hora = it takes an hour to get there.

target: Ni que fueras su madre para hablarle así.
english: You're not his mother to talk to him like that.
tip: Ni que fueras su madre = as if you were his mother! Ni que + past subjunctive mocks an absurd assumption – sarcasm built straight into the mood system.

target: Se dice que van a abrir un supermercado nuevo.
english: They say they're going to open a new supermarket.
tip: "Se dice que..." = It is said that. Impersonal se for common knowledge or rumors.

target: No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.
english: It's not that I don't want to, it's that I can't.
tip: No es que + subjunctive is the excuse formula: quiera bends because you're batting that idea away as false; the real reason – es que no puedo – stays plain indicative.

target: La profesora pidió que los padres asistieran a la reunión.
english: The teacher asked that the parents attend the meeting.
tip: Asistieran is a false friend: asistir a = to attend, be present at. The parents aren't helping run the meeting – to assist someone is ayudar.

target: ¿Has probado la nueva cafetería?
english: Have you tried the new café?
tip: Probado, because probar = try by tasting or testing a thing. Attempt an action? That's intentar. A new café is something you sample – pure probar.

target: ¿Habrá llegado ya el pedido?
english: Do you think the order has arrived yet?
tip: ¿Habrá llegado? isn't about the future – Spanish borrows future forms to guess about now: it-will-have-arrived = it's probably arrived, don't you think?

target: Ojalá mi familia viviera más cerca.
english: I wish my family lived closer.
tip: Ojalá comes from Arabic law sha Allah, God willing – a holdover from Moorish al-Andalus. It always takes subjunctive: ojalá viviera.

target: A propósito, ¿has visto a María últimamente?
english: By the way, have you seen María lately?
tip: A propósito has two meanings: opening a sentence it's by the way; after a verb (lo hizo a propósito) it's on purpose. Position picks the meaning.

target: Si reservamos ahora, nos saldrá más barato.
english: If we book now, it will be cheaper for us.
tip: "Salir" used impersonally: "nos saldrá" = it will come out to / it will cost us.

target: La mantequilla se ha derretido con el calor.
english: The butter has melted in the heat.
tip: Nobody melted the butter – it just happened, and Spanish marks blameless events with se: se ha derretido. Same no-fault se as se rompió, se cayó.

target: El recibo dice que me han cobrado de más.
english: The receipt says I've been overcharged.
tip: Spanish dodges the passive with a vague they: me han cobrado de más – literally they've charged me in excess = I've been overcharged. The they is no one in particular.

target: El proyecto en el que estoy trabajando es complicado.
english: The project I'm working on is complicated.
tip: English strands the preposition: 'the project I'm working ON.' Spanish doesn't allow that – en moves to the front along with el que: en el que estoy trabajando.
